passage: Sunday night Imran's report card is on the table and I keep looking at it. Maths and reading marked "needs support" again. At lunch Bhabhi said, loud enough for him to hear, "Our Pihu reads English novels already." Imran went quiet and pushed his rice around. Part of me wanted to book the strict tuition teacher the whole colony talks about. Part of me wanted to hide him from everyone. Instead I rang his class teacher and asked for a meeting. She said the school can help with extra reading time. Then I pinned his clay elephant on the fridge photo wall and told him it's the best one in the building. He slept with the report card under his pillow. I don't know why. I'll ask tomorrow. - Charu (his very tired mother)

qa.q: Where did Charu put a picture of Imran's clay elephant?
qa.a: On the fridge photo wall.

qa.q: What was Charu worried about after the report card, and why did it feel like a pull in two directions?
qa.a: Charu was torn between pushing Imran with strict tuition and protecting him from everyone's comments.

qa.q: Which choice helped keep the family steady?
qa.a: Charu rang the class teacher to plan help with the school, and also celebrated Imran's clay elephant.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt when Bhabhi talked about Pihu?
qa.a: He probably felt compared and small; he went quiet and pushed his rice around.

grounding: It shows a parent who worries about grades and relatives' comments, feels torn between pushing and protecting, and works with the school while praising her child's other talents.

passage: In the milk queue outside the dairy, Patil-kaka asked Darshan loudly, "So your Zubin still can't read the bus board?" A few people laughed. Darshan's face went hot. All the way home he argued with himself. Send the boy to the tuition master in the next town, three hours a day? Or keep him home, away from these remarks? That evening he sat with Zubin, who was sanding a little wooden bullock cart for his cousin. The wheels actually turned. "You made this without a drawing?" Darshan asked. "I saw it in my head, Papa." Next morning Darshan went to the school, not the tuition master. The teacher agreed to sit with them both every Saturday. At the village fair, the wooden cart won a ribbon, and Darshan stood right beside it.

qa.q: What was Zubin sanding in the evening?
qa.a: A little wooden bullock cart for his cousin.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel after the comment in the milk queue, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and torn; his face went hot and he argued with himself all the way home.

qa.q: What turning point settled Darshan's choice?
qa.a: Seeing Zubin build the cart from his head made him go to the school to work with the teacher instead of the long tuition.

qa.q: How does Zubin likely feel when his father stands beside the cart at the fair?
qa.a: He probably feels proud and backed by his father, seeing his talent valued in front of the village.

grounding: It shows a father worried by others' comments, torn between pushing and protecting, who works with the school and celebrates his son's other talent.

passage:
Thursday night.
Saurabh's report card came today. Maths: 34. I am his mother, and I sat on the bed and felt sick. At the lift, Mrs Bhatia said her son "just does tuition, simple." I smiled and wanted to scream.
Part of me wants to sit with him for two hours every night and drill tables. Part of me wants to hide the report and tell him marks don't matter. Neither feels right.
I met his class teacher after school. She said he tries hard and suggested the school's learning support twice a week. We agreed to try.
Then Saurabh showed me the clay temple he made for art. Every tiny bell. I put it on the TV shelf where everyone will see it.

qa.q: What mark did Saurabh get in maths?
qa.a: He got 34 in maths.

qa.q: How did the mother feel about pushing or protecting Saurabh?
qa.a: She felt torn and anxious, wanting both to drill him every night and to hide the report and tell him marks don't matter.

qa.q: What steps help keep the family steady?
qa.a: Meeting the class teacher, agreeing to try learning support and proudly displaying Saurabh's clay temple to celebrate his talent.

qa.q: How might Saurabh feel seeing the clay temple on the TV shelf?
qa.a: Saurabh may feel proud and valued, knowing his mother celebrates what he is good at, not only his maths marks.

grounding: Shows a parent worried about grades and others' comments, torn between pushing and protecting, who works with the school and celebrates her child's other talent.

passage: At the family lunch in Udvada, Zubin's aunt looked at Reena's notebook and clicked her tongue. "Nine years old and still can't do sums? In our day we got a slap." Reena slid under the table with her plate. Zubin felt his face heat. That night, closing the bakery, he wondered whether he should make her do extra sums before bed, or just let her be. In the morning he walked to the school and sat with her teacher, who showed him how Reena counted on her fingers under the desk. They made a plan: counters at home, no timed tests for now. On the way back Reena sang the whole bakery jingle she had made up, and Zubin sang it with her.

qa.q: Where did Zubin sit with Reena's teacher?
qa.a: He walked to the school in the morning and sat with her teacher there.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel after his aunt's comment?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and torn, his face heating, unsure whether to push Reena with extra sums or just let her be.

qa.q: What did Zubin do that was wise?
qa.a: He worked with the teacher on a clear plan, counters at home and no timed tests for now, instead of reacting to his aunt.

qa.q: What was the family lunch like for Reena?
qa.a: It was probably humiliating and frightening, which is why she slid under the table with her plate.

grounding: Shows a parent hurt by a relative's comment and torn between pushing and protecting, who works with the school and enjoys his child's other talents.

passage: In Berlin, Selin read the class chat on her phone: another parent had posted the maths results, "Proud of our girl, top again!" Selin put the phone face down. Ines, eight, had cried over her number homework for an hour. Selin wanted to hire a tutor for every afternoon; she also wanted to write to the school and say, "Leave her alone." Instead she asked for a meeting. The teacher suggested blocks at home and extra help on Wednesdays, and told her Ines explained football tactics better than anyone. That weekend Selin stood by the pitch and cheered every pass Ines made. At home, the maths blocks sat on the kitchen table, ready for ten minutes a day.

qa.q: How long had Ines cried over her number homework?
qa.a: She had cried over her number homework for an hour.

qa.q: How did Selin feel reading the other parent's post?
qa.a: She felt hurt and anxious, putting the phone face down while comparing it with Ines's struggle.

qa.q: Which choice helped Selin more than hiring a daily tutor or confronting the school?
qa.a: Asking for a meeting and working with the teacher on blocks at home and extra help on Wednesdays.

qa.q: How might Ines experience her mother cheering at the pitch?
qa.a: Ines may feel confident and loved, seeing that her mother is proud of her football even when maths is hard.

grounding: Shows a parent worried by grades and comparisons, torn between pushing and protecting, who works with the school and celebrates her child's talent.

passage:
At the parent-teacher meeting, Tanuja sat on the small plastic chair clutching Mahima's report card. Science: 42. English: 38.
In the corridor, another mother had just said, "Tuition every day, that's what she needs." Tanuja's face still burned.
"I don't know whether to push her harder or protect her," she told Mrs Kapoor, the class teacher. "She cries over spellings every night."
Mrs Kapoor opened a folder. "The special educator has noticed she mixes letters. We can give her extra time and oral tests. But look here." She showed a drawing from art class, a detailed map of their colony, every house labelled with pictures.
Tanuja laughed through wet eyes. "She draws all day."
"Then let's make sure she knows she's good at something," said Mrs Kapoor. They set a meeting with the educator for Monday.

qa.q: What mark did Mahima get in English?
How did Tanuja feel after the other mother's comment?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and anxious, her face still burning, and torn between pushing Mahima and protecting her.

qa.q: What steps helped Tanuja feel steadier?
qa.a: Working with the school's special educator on extra time and oral tests, and celebrating Mahima's talent for drawing to keep her confidence up.

qa.q: What is it like for Mahima at home in the evenings?
qa.a: She seems frustrated and upset, crying over spellings every night, which is why protecting her confidence matters.

grounding: Tanuja, worried about grades and comments, is torn between pushing and protecting, and working with the school and celebrating her daughter's talent steadies her.
